title: Es-saa‘a kam — time, days and appointments
goal: Tell the time the Levantine way, name the days and parts of the day, and make a simple appointment — including the "half seven" trap.
bekal: ask and say what time it is
name the days of the week and the parts of the day
make an appointment with a clear time and day

dialogs.title: حَكِي — مَوْعِد بُكْرَا
dialogs.intro: Samer invites Budi on a walk through the old city, and the two of them settle on a time.

lines.speaker: سَامِر:
lines.text: إِيه، اَلتَّلَاتَا. بَدِّي نْرُوح عَ الْبَلَد الْقَدِيمِة.
lines.baca: ēh, et-talaata. baddi nruuh ‘a el-balad el-’adiime.
lines.id: Yes, Tuesday. I'd like us to go to the old city.
lines.literal: yes, Tuesday. want-my we-go to the-city the-old.

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.text: بَكِّير شْوَي. عِنْدِي صَفّ لَلْعَشَرَة وْنُصّ.
lines.baca: bakkiir shway. ‘indi ṣaff la-el-‘ashara w nuṣṣ.
lines.id: A bit early. I have class until half past ten.
lines.literal: early a-little. at-me class until-ten and half.

lines.speaker: سَامِر:
lines.id: In front of the Umayyad Mosque. Do you know it?

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.id: I know it. But don't be late.

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.text: إِنْ شَاءَ اللَّه. لَلْكَم بِنْضَلّ هْنِيك؟
lines.id: Let's hope. Until what time will we stay there?
lines.literal: if God wills. until-how-much we-stay there?

lines.speaker: سَامِر:
lines.baca: laba‘d eḍ-ḍuhr. bnaakul hniik w bnirja‘.
lines.id: Until the afternoon. We'll eat there and come back.
lines.literal: until-after the-noon. we-eat there and we-return.

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.baca: maashi. bshuufak bukra el-hda‘sh w rubi‘.
lines.id: OK. See you tomorrow at a quarter past eleven.
lines.literal: walking. I-see-you tomorrow eleven and quarter.

notes: **⚠️ Arabic counts the half hour FORWARD.** The phrase اَلسَّاعَة سِتِّة وْنُصّ means **6:30** — just like British "half six". If your own language (German, Dutch, Scandinavian, Polish…) says "half seven" for 6:30, this is your number-one trap, and it costs you an hour on every appointment.

**Minutes are added with وْ and taken away with إِلَّا.** The form وْرُبِع means "a quarter past", إِلَّا رُبِع means "a quarter to". Only four are used all the time: وْرُبِع، وْنُصّ، إِلَّا رُبِع، وْعَشَرَة.
**Days of the week take اَل in front.** The forms are اَلتَّلَاتَا (Tuesday), اَلْأَرْبَعَا (Wednesday). Dropping اَل sounds like reading a calendar, not talking.

**The Levantine week starts on Sunday, and the days off vary.** In Syria and Jordan the weekend is Friday and Saturday. In Lebanon, Saturday and Sunday. This isn't about language, but it decides when the shops are closed.

**Parts of the day are often marked by prayer times, even by people who don't pray.** The phrases قَبِل الْمَغْرِب and بَعِد الضُّهِر are used every day by everyone, including in religiously mixed Lebanon. They work as neutral time markers.
**The word لَا in front of a verb means "don't".** The form لَا تْتَأَخَّر means "don't be late". We cover it fully in unit 16; for now, just recognize that لَا + verb = a prohibition.

grammars.title: Telling the time
after: ⚠️ Once more, because this is what goes wrong most often: **وْنُصّ means half PAST.** The time سِتِّة وْنُصّ is 6:30. If you mean 5:30, say خَمْسِة وْنُصّ.
To make morning or evening clear, add الصُّبِح (morning), بَعِد الضُّهِر (midday), الْعَصِر (afternoon) or اَلْمَسَا (evening) after it. The 24-hour clock is almost never used in conversation.

grammars.title: Days and parts of the day
after: Time words that go with them: اَلْيَوْم *el-yōm* (today), بُكْرَا *bukra* (tomorrow), مْبَارِح *mbaarih* (yesterday), بَعِد بُكْرَا *ba‘d bukra* (the day after tomorrow), وَّل مْبَارِح *awwal mbaarih* (the day before yesterday).

⚠️ The word غَدَا *ghada* means **lunch**, not "tomorrow" — even though in Fusha غَدًا does mean tomorrow. It's a direct trap for anyone who has studied Fusha: a lunch invitation can sound like a plan for tomorrow.

blocks.text: The phrase اِتَّفَقْنَا is the neatest way to seal an agreement on a time, and it works like a handshake. After it, people usually don't confirm the time again — except you, who as a beginner should still repeat it once.

blocks.title: ⚠️ Time in the Levant is more relaxed
items: A social meeting at seven often means somewhere between seven and half past, and that's no sign of disrespect. Work meetings and doctor's appointments, on the other hand, are kept.
If you need precision, add بِالضَّبْط *biḍ-ḍabṭ* ("exactly"): اَلسَّاعَة سَبْعَة بِالضَّبْط. Everyone understands that as a serious request.
Saying إِنْ شَاءَ اللَّه about an appointment **doesn't always mean "yes"**. Often it means "hopefully", with a chance it won't happen. If you need certainty, ask again: يَعْنِي أَكِيد؟

blocks.text: The word سَاعَة does double duty: it means "clock, watch", "hour" as a unit of time, and it opens a time phrase as in اَلسَّاعَة كَم. Only context tells them apart, and it's never confusing.

blocks.title: Saying how long something lasts
items: For a length of time, say the number followed by the unit: تْلَات سَاعَات (three hours), عَشْر دَقَايِق (ten minutes).
For "since" or "ago", use مِن *min*: مِن سَاعَة (an hour ago), مِن شَهْر (for a month).
For "until", use لَـ *la-*: لَلْعَشَرَة (until ten o'clock), لَبُكْرَا (until tomorrow).

exercises.prompt: Write the time in Levantine Arabic.
Put the words in the right order.

answers: اَلسَّاعَة كَم؟ — اَلسَّاعَة تِسْعَة وْرُبِع. — بْنِلْتِقِي بُكْرَا السَّاعَة حْدَعْش. — عِنْدِي صَفّ لَلْوَحْدِة. — يَوْم الْجُمْعَة أَنَا فَاضِي. — لَا تْتَأَخَّر.
اَلسَّاعَة تْمَانْيِة — اَلسَّاعَة تْمَانْيِة وْرُبِع — اَلسَّاعَة تْمَانْيِة وْنُصّ — اَلسَّاعَة تِسْعَة إِلَّا رُبِع — اَلسَّاعَة عَشَرَة وْعَشَرَة — اَلسَّاعَة تْنَعْش
وْنُصّ — إِلَّا — بُكْرَا — اَلتَّلَاتَا — اَلصُّبِح — اِتَّفَقْنَا
اَلسَّاعَة كَم؟ — اَلسَّاعَة سَبْعَة وْنُصّ. — إِمْتَى بْنِلْتِقِي؟ — بُكْرَا فَاضِي؟ — بْنِلْتِقِي قِدَّام الْجَامِع. — لَا تْتَأَخَّر.
wave: Look at your watch six times today and say the time out loud in Levantine Arabic. Remember: وْنُصّ means half past.
